Abstract – Machine learning based sentiment analysis is an 
interdisciplinary approach in opinion mining, particularly in the 
field of media and communication research. In spite of their 
different backgrounds, researchers have collaborated to test, train 
and again retest the machine learning approach to collect, analyse 
and withdraw a meaningful insight from large datasets. This 
research classifies the texts of micro-blog (tweets) into positive and 
negative responses about a particular phenomenon. The study also 
demonstrates the process of compilation of corpus for review of 
sentiments, cleaning the body of text to make it a meaningful text, 
find people’s emotions about it, and interpret the findings. Till 
date the public sentiment after abrogation of Article 370 has not 
been studied, which adds the novelty to this scientific study. This 
study includes the dataset collection from Twitter that comprises 
66.7 % of positive tweets and 34.3 % of negative tweets of the 
people about the abrogation of Article 370. Experimental testing 
reveals that the proposed methodology is much more effective than 
the previously proposed methodology. This study focuses on 
comparison of unsupervised lexicon-based models (TextBlob, 
AFINN, Vader Sentiment) and supervised machine learning 
models (KNN, SVM, Random Forest and Naïve Bayes) for 
sentiment analysis. This is the first study with cyber public opinion 
over the abrogation of Article 370. Twitter data of more than 2 
lakh tweets were collected by the authors. After cleaning, 29732 
tweets were selected for analysis. As per the results among 
supervised learning, Random Forest performs the best, whereas 
among unsupervised learning TextBlob achieves the highest 
accuracy of 99 % and 88 %, respectively. Performance 
parameters of the proposed supervised machine learning models 
also surpass the result of the recent study performed in 2023 for 
sentiment analysis. 
 
Keywords – Article 370, machine learning, natural language 
processing, sentiment analysis, Twitter API. 
I. INTRODUCTION 
With the advancement in rapid communication system and 
popularity of micro-blogging platforms, netizens are freely 
expressing their views in their day-to-day life on blogging sites 
like Facebook, Twitter etc. These are the popular platforms for 
users to share their views and viewpoints on various types of 
goods, services, individuals and debates particularly in favour

or against, and so on. Such micro blogs on social media like 
Twitter are becoming an influential platform to generate any 
kind of publicity for and against of any phenomenon. In India, 
the Narendra Modi led Union Government of India revoked 
Article 370 that gave special status for the Jammu and Kashmir, 
which led to huge hue and cry in the media. Media rhetoric and 
public sentiments were divided into positive and negative 
responses in terms of their reactions. The right wing supporters 
celebrated the revocation of Article 370 with full enthusiasm & 
zeal; the Modi Fandoms called abrogation of Article 370 a 
historic and appreciable decision. But, at the same time, the 
decision of abrogation of Article 370 was criticized by centrally 
left or left oriented party, and a retired judge of the apex court. 
Justice Gopal Gowda, former judge of Supreme Court of India, 
described the decision of abrogation of Article 370 as the 
violation of constitution [1]. Preventive detention was also 
taken as precautionary measure; Jammu and Kashmir 
administration had detained several political leaders, including 
three former Chief Ministers, to avoid any reactionary 
movement after the revocation of Article 370 in the valley [2]. 
According to the official statement of right wing leader and 
general secretary of BJP, Ram Madhav, earlier two thousand to 
twenty five hundred people were detained but later on numbers 
were reduced to two hundred approximately [2]. On the other 
hand, Left Wing Leader Brinda Karat & Sita Ram Yechuri 
demanded the immediate release of detained political leaders.  
CPI (M) General Secretary led to a protest at Jantar Mantar, 
condemning the Modi government for scrapping of Article 370 
and asked Government of India to restore the statehood status 
of Jammu and Kashmir [3]. As per the media reports, 
researchers were witnessing mixed sentiments on abrogation of 
Article 370 from the people of different ideologies and 
backgrounds. 
Thus, 
such 
divided 
opinions 
motivated 
researchers to conduct a sentiment analysis, by using machine 
learning techniques, to measure the mixed opinion. Sentiment 
analysis is a technique of understanding the positive and 
negative response of the people, by analysing the textual 
material like blogs, tweets and e-mails.

On a particular topic, people generate favourable opinion 
then debate, discuss and criticize, as per their own choice and 
likings, especially on social media sites like Twitter, Facebook,

Most of the internet users have shifted to micro blogging 
services from conventional networking resources (such as

For sentiment analysis, researchers have used a mixed approach 
of utilizing the machine learning, use of common lexicon [4] to 
identify the positive and negative words, hybridization 
approach to identify its meaning in real sense. This case of 
Abrogation of Article 370 is taken for the testing of technique 
as an experimental dataset. 
The main objective of adopting this approach is to 
understand twitter users’ reactions in the case of Article 370 
abrogation. Another major objective is to test the possibility of 
using supervised machine learning approach to mine the 
opinion of twitter users in media and communication research 
by labelling the data using various unsupervised learning 
approaches.  For the above purpose, researchers have gathered 
the data of more than twenty-nine thousand tweets to perform 
the sentiment analysis of abrogation of Article 370. The authors 
have trained and tested the various machine-learning models to 
conduct the analysis of gathered tweets on #Article370. 
In this research, a keyword-based tweet set under abrogation 
#Article370 was setup to understand the popularity of the 
Article 370 among the twitter users. Initially, supervised and 
unsupervised machine learning algorithms were adopted to test 
the dataset. In unsupervised classification, the following 
analytical techniques were used: TextBlob, AFINN and Vader 
Sentiment and in supervised learning: KNN, SVM, Random 
Forest and Naïve Bayes were used to identify the emotions. The 
accuracy of each model was demonstrated and tested. 
1. TextBlob Module: The module TextBlob [5] helps us to 
use the positive and negative labels. Every word in a 
corpus is classified in terms of polarity and subjectivity 
(there are also more marks, but we will disregard them 
for now). The sum of these is a feeling of a corpus. 
Polarity describes positive and negative meanings of a 
word; meaningfully −1 is defined as very negative. +1 is 
defined as very positive. 
Subjectivity 
describes 
a 
word’s 
subjectivity 
or 
opinionated and faithfulness. 0 is defined as a fact and 
+1 is defined as opinion. 
2. AFINN Module: The AFINN lexicon [6] is perhaps one 
of the simplest and most common lexicons which is most 
extensively used for the sentiment analysis. The AFINN 
lexicon is a list of English phrases which were manually 
graded for valence with an integer between −5 
(negative) and +5 (positive). Finn Årup Nielsen between 
2009 and 2011 evaluated a word list for sentiment 
analysis in micro blogs. 
3. Vader Sentiment Module: VADER-Valence Aware 
Dictionary and Emotion Reasoner [7] is a lexicon and 
rule-based analytical tool geared specifically for social 
media sentiments; it is quite sensitive to both cognitive 
(positive/negative) and strength (fortitude) polarity. 
Analysis of the VADER plain text sentiment uses a 
normal human-centred approach, combining qualitative 
research with an objective assessment by using 
individual raters and crowd wisdom. This follows a 
lexicon-based approach in which researchers do not train 
a model; this gives a freedom using labelled data, from 
dictionary of emotions to determine the feeling of 
sentences. 
4. Supervised Machine Learning Module: The identical 
dataset evaluates the use of Supervised Machine 
Learning Algorithms. On the other hand [8], 
unsupervised machine learning techniques look at 
previously labelled data to assess the feeling of never 
seen before sentences. The approach of machine 
learning involves training the model to predict or 
categorize the feeling of any regular text input using 
previously trained text. The positive aspect about 
machine learning approaches is that it generally gets 
better predictive or classification results within a larger 
volume of data. In this work, KNN, SVM, Random 
Forest and Naïve Bayes algorithms were used under the 
supervised learning techniques. 
Contribution to Research: The major contribution of the 
study includes: 
a) This study is also unique in its terms of data (first-hand 
information) and collection time, which was done during 
the second and third weeks of August. It was collected 
immediately after the announcement of abrogation by 
the Government, i.e., on 5 August 2019. 
b) Study of people’s emotions in regards to abrogation of 
Article 370 by labelling of polarity and sentiment of 
collected data. 
c) Current study includes the performance comparison of 
supervised (KNN, Random Forest, SVM and Naïve 
Bayes) and unsupervised (TextBlob, AFINN and Vader 
Sentiment) algorithms for people’s emotions. 
d) Results were compared with the recent studies for 
performance analysis of machine learning models. 
II. LITERATURE REVIEW 
Twitter users are aggressively participating in debates and 
discussions over the electoral politics in India and around the 
world, which usually triggers the flow of communication and 
helps in generating sentiments. Twitter plays an important role 
in electoral sentiments. One of the studies by [9] gathered hash 
tag-based tweets masking Indian 2014 election candidates. 
They did not provide neutral tweets for the study due to the fact 
they considered such sorts of tweets to be difficult to analyse in 
terms of feelings that help one group. Particularly, for 
concluding the sentiment analysis of tweets, two lexicons were 
merged successfully [10]–[12]. In the case of a two-part study, 
this bipolar lexicon performed well. However, they generated 
variables for the classification of a couple of events and their 
methodology was not ultra-modern to measure sentiment score.

The researchers used TextBlob [13] to measure polarity and 
polarity confidence. They used SVM and Naïve Bayes in 
WEKA to validate the tests. They registered Naïve Bayes with 
very good accuracy at a price of 65.2 %, which used to be 5.1 % 
higher than SVM precision levels. An unsupervised machine-
learning algorithm [8] was used to be applied to see the remarks 
as thumbs up and down; 410 remarks were bought from 
Opinions and tested. The calculated algorithm accuracy was 
74 % in the study. The authors [14], [15] analysed SVM and 
Naïve Bayes sentiments about political events for the prediction 
of elections of India and the USA. The study was performed in 
2016 and predicted the BJP’s electoral probabilities to prevail 
with accuracy of 78.4 % using the SVM test, which was 16.3 % 
higher than the Naïve Bayesian performance. In addition, the 
authors [16] used the proposed technique for higher forecasts of 
elections based on public opinion from internet forums, 
resulting in accuracy of 83 %. 
Twitter sentiment analysis was also conducted on the tweet 
data regarding demonetisation of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 
banknotes by the Indian government. In a study conducted 
by [17], researcher gathered hashtag tweets and after collecting 
the tweets, researcher applied the sentiment evaluation 
technique to analyse the data. Sentiment evaluation API was 
used, which could be applied in MS Excel as an add-in. API 
produced the following results: P+ (strongly positive), P 
(strongly negative), N+ (strongly negative) and N (neutral). In 
early stages, the results indicated that twitter users completely 
supported this decision, but when they began to face difficulties 
about banknote non-availability, people’s emotions flipped to 
negative side. In this study, sentiments analysis mainly 
depended on SentiWordNet. The framework discussed in this 
research paper purely relied on SentiWordNet (an opinion 
mining lexical tool [18]). In SentiWordNet, ratings are assigned 
to every WordNet synset, i.e., a score of positiveness, negativity 
and objectivity. Such scores are usually summed to 1. The triple 
{0, 1, 0} (positivity, negativity, objectivity), for example, is 
allocated to the synset of the word ‘bad’. In this synset, the sum 
of all rankings in SentiWordNet was once robotically generated 
through a combination of language classification and statistics. 
This combination produced a good number of personal opinion-
related tasks with accurate results, i.e., for subjectivity 
assessment and sentiment analysis. The study by Devitt and 
Ahmad 2007 [19] used this technique for sentiment polarity 
detection. Their lexicon-based strategy primarily focused on the 
software of SentiWordNet to measure good and poor 
sentiments. In conjunction with WordNet Affect, Chaumartin’s 
linguistic rule-based approach [10] makes use of SentiWordNet 
to identify emotions and valence for words in media. This was 
used only in a monolingual context and in a monolingual 
framework. Subjective adjectives from SentiWordNet are 
derived [20]. Instead, these adjectives are used as 
characteristics to estimate the likelihood that a textual content 
contains expressions of opinion. 
Recent study by Verma Pankaj and Jamwal Sanjay [21] has 
examined the sentiments of various Indian Government policies 
(namely, Article 370, New Motor Vehicles Act 2019, Triple 
Talaq, Jal Shakti Abhiyan, NRC Assam) on Twitter so that 
public opinions and views are analysed. Emotions (anger, trust, 
fear, anticipation, disgust, sadness, joy, surprise) are analysed 
using emotion-based lexicon technique. Sentiments are 
classified into two categories (positive and negative) from the 
emotion lexicon EmoLex. The study has only taken up the 
percentage of people in a particular emotion group but has not 
performed any analysis with any of the supervised and 
unsupervised techniques. 
One of the inspirations of the current study is of Kumar and 
Singh [14]. This study covered the fake news analysis. In this 
study, the authors used the comprehensive way of detecting 
fake news using a machine learning model. Model in the study 
is trained by Fake News data based on the US election and 
trained on recent Indian political fake news. In this study, 
sentiments are precleaned or pre-processed to extract the 
meaningful information. The study used the supervised and 
unsupervised techniques to analyse the tweets.   
Ali Hassan [22] has performed the sentiment analysis with 
the two major machine learning algorithms, i.e., Naïve Bayes 
and SVM. They collected the dataset of 100 000 tweets and 
after pre-processing there remained 6250 tweets. Results of 
Naïve Bayes showed the maximum accuracy of 79 % with W-
WSD polarity calculation. Further in case of SVM it achieved 
maximum accuracy of 62.33 % using W-WSD. The study had 
very limited dataset collection and used only two Ml algorithms 
for analysis. 
Upon conducting an extensive examination of the existing 
literature, it has been identified that there are several research 
gaps that demand further investigation. These gaps are outlined 
as follows: 
1. Non-availability of a large dataset of people’s 
sentiments (through Twitter) for abrogation of 
Article 370 day after the announcement. 
2. Study of public emotions for abrogation of Article 370. 
3. Performance achieved by the available studies for 
sentiment analysis with the proposed methodologies is 
low (less than 80 % of accuracy). 
4. Very limited study for the comparison of unsupervised 
(lexical) and supervised machine learning algorithms is 
available for sentiment analysis. 
III. PROPOSED METHODOLOGY FOR CLASSIFICATION 
The current study described a cycle from selection, 
evaluating emotions and classifying Twitter opinions 
depending upon the polarity. The study considered user-posted 
tweets in hashtag form to share their views on the repeal of 
Article 370. Then, the collected tweets were stored in the 
database, and the dataset was pre-processed. Polarity and 
subjectivity were measured after pre-processing of data. These 
were classified using unsupervised and supervised learning 
techniques. Under unsupervised techniques, three methods 
were 
used: 
TextBlob [23], 
AFINN [6], 
and 
Vader 
Sentiment [7]. For classification in supervised learning, the 
KNN, SVM, Random Forest and Naïve Bayes were used for 
training and testing the classification.  Classifiers were selected 
because of heterogeneity nature of collected data. Further, the 
prediction class is categorical (positive, negative and neutral)

Pre-processing is the most important stage to omit the useless 
and unwanted data. During the pre-processing stage, as per 
study requirement the meaningless Twitter data [24] were 
removed with the following exclusion criteria: 
• 
Eliminating URLs: URL validation can be done using 
the regular expression (http-zA-Z0- 9\\./]+. 
• 
Eliminating Handles (User Reference): Handles with 
normal expression can be eliminated-@(\w+). 
• 
Removing hash tags: Hash tags can be eliminated by 
searching expression - #(\w+). 
• 
Emoticon elimination: Users can also use emoticon 
vocabulary to filter out the emoticons or store their 
appearance in a distinctive script. 
• 
Eliminating recurring characters. 
• 
Eliminating the duplicate and non-relevant tweets.

C. Polarity Calculation and Sentiment Analysis 
Sentiment evaluation may also grant beneficial insights from 
social media web sites with the aid of identifying emotions or 
ideas in unstructured layout from a massive volume of 
information present on Twitter. Analysis of sentiment has three 
types of polarity: negative, neutral and positive. A tweet 
polarity is calculated by assigning a score from −1 to +1. A poor 
score means a bad feeling, and a fantastic rating means a 
tremendous feeling, while the zero ranking is regarded as 
neutral feeling. Our study disregarded all neutral tweets, so the 
study tried to get the opinion on the basis of positive and 
negative sentiments only. A subjectivity rating assigned to 
every tweet was primarily based on whether or not it reflected 
a mean or a goal meaning; the subjectivity score range was also 
from 0 to 1. Tweets that held a ranking above 0 was objective 
and close to 1 was subjective. Partial representation of data after 
assigning a score is demonstrated in Fig. 2.

TextBlob starts with the basic points of natural language 
processing; the study used this analyser to measure polarity and 
subjectivity tweets as follows. 
Polarity: To understand whether a tweet is positive or negative, 
e.g., −1 is very negative; +1 is very positive. 
Subjectivity: To understand the subjectivity or opinionated a 
word, e.g., 0 is fact; +1 is very much an opinion. 
Lexicon on AFINN is a listing of English phrases for an integer 
of −5 (negative) to + 5 (positive) hand-rated for valence. 
Vader Sentiment Module: VADER (Valence Aware Dictionary 
and sentiment reasoner) is a lexicon-based strategy; this module 
has a trained model that uses the labelled data. It has the 
complete data and its meaning, one only needs to determine the 
feeling through the emotion dictionary. 
D. Supervised Machine Learning Methodology 
Supervised machine learning approach seems to have 
beforehand labelled information to determine the feeling of 
sentences, which has never been determined earlier. This was 
obtained from the above mentioned unsupervised models. Here 
is how a machine-learning classifier works with labelled 
information: 
1. Training-Prediction Processes: This method learns to link 
a particular input (i.e., a text). The extractor function transfers 
the input text to a feature vector. To construct a model, the 
machine-learning algorithm is fed with sets of vectors and tags 
(e.g., positive and negative). Such feature vectors were loaded 
into another model and expected tags (positive and negative) 
were generated for using them in research. 
2. Feature Extraction from Text: New feature extraction 
methods primarily based on word embedding (also known as 
phrase vectors) have been introduced more recently. This form 
of representations permits terms with similar means to have a 
comparable representation, which can boost classifier 
efficiency. 
3. Classification of Text: The classification system divided 
the text based on feature extracted with a statistical model like

Pseudo-Code of Algorithm for Classification: 
As per the proposed methodology discussed in Fig. 1a, the 
following is the algorithmic view of the solution for sentiment 
analysis:  
 
Step 1: Data Pre-processing 
1. Load and pre-process the dataset of tweets (e.g., 
tokenization, lowercasing, removing stop words, etc.). 
2. Split the dataset into training and testing sets. 
 
Step 2: Feature Extraction 
3. Convert the pre-processed text data into numerical feature 
vectors. 
4. Assign sentiment labels to the feature vectors (positive or 
negative) based on sentiment of each tweet in the training set. 
 
Step 3: Model Training 
5. Train the machine learning model on the training set. 
a. Use the feature vectors as input features and sentiment 
labels as the target variable. 
b. Tune hyperparameters of each model, for example, in case 
of SVM the kernel type, regularization parameter, etc. 
 
Step 4. Sentiment Analysis 
6. Apply the trained model to predict sentiment labels for the 
feature vectors of the testing set. 
a. Use the learned model to classify the feature vectors into 
positive or negative sentiment. 
b. Generate predicted sentiment labels for the testing set. 
 
Step 5. Evaluation 
7. Compare the predicted sentiment labels with the ground truth 
sentiment labels of the testing set to evaluate the performance 
of the sentiment analysis model. 
a. Compute evaluation metrics such as accuracy, precision, 
recall, F1-score, to measure the model performance.

V. CONCLUSION 
The 
research 
focused on 
sentiment 
analysis 
with 
unsupervised lexicon-based approach and supervised machine 
learning approach. The study was performed to check the 
accuracy for sentiment analysis with an aspect focus on tweets 
related to abrogation of Article 370. More than 29 thousand 
(29732) tweets were analysed from the collection set of 2 lakh 
tweets during the second and third weeks of August 2019. It 
was collected immediately after the announcement of 
Government for abrogation of Article 370, i.e., 5 August 2019. 
Among the selected tweets, there were 66.7 % of positive 
tweets and 34.3 % of negative tweets. Polarity in lexicon-based 
strategy was determined based on a dictionary consisting of a 
semantic rating of given words. However, the major 
contribution that added novelty to the study includes the 
following: 
1. To collect the tweets (more than 2 lakh) and label them 
with lexicon-based polarity methods. After cleaning, 
29732 tweets were selected. 
2. The polarity based tagging of selected tweets was done 
with positive and negative sentiments as input for 
supervised machine learning algorithms. 
3. Further, another contribution was to provide comparison 
between the lexicon of sentiments (AFINN, Vader 
Sentiment, TextBlob) and machine learning techniques 
(KNN, SVM, Random Forest and Naïve Bayes) so that 
the best sentiment analysis technique could be adopted 
for analysing the tweets. 
4. In the analysis, the supervised learning surpassed the 
unsupervised learning with a score of 99 % for 
Accuracy, Recall, Precision, F1 and AUC values. In 
supervised learning, Random Forest achieved the 
highest 
score 
for 
each 
performance 
parameter 
(Accuracy, Precision, Recall and F1), i.e., 98 % and 
99 % in case of AUC of ROC. On the other hand, in 
unsupervised learning TextBlob outcomes were slightly 
better in each value of performance parameters 
(Accuracy, Recall, Precision and F1), i.e., 88 %, 91 %, 
88 % and 89 %, respectively. 
5. The research compared the results of the recent studies 
[13], [27] (Table III), which implemented similar 
machine learning algorithms (like SVM, LR, RF). As 
per the results of the current study, it shows the best 
results for Accuracy, Precision, Recall and F1 with value 
of 99 % for Random Forest. This adds the novelty to the 
process adopted for sentiment analysis. 
In this research, researchers received favourable results in 
forming an opinion on classification of tweets on the basis of 
polarity for abrogation of Article 370.

Abstract: – Machine learning based sentiment analysis is an interdisciplinary approach in opinion mining, particularly in the field of media and communication research. In spite of their different backgrounds, researchers have collaborated to test, train and again retest the machine learning approach to collect, analyse and withdraw a meaningful insight from large datasets. This research classifies the texts of micro-blog (tweets) into positive and negative responses about a particular phenomenon. The study also demonstrates the process of compilation of corpus for review of sentiments, cleaning the body of text to make it a meaningful text, find people’s emotions about it, and interpret the findings. Till date the public sentiment after abrogation of Article 370 has not been studied, which adds the novelty to this scientific study. This study includes the dataset collection from Twitter that comprises 66.7 % of positive tweets and 34.3 % of negative tweets of the people about the abrogation of Article 370. Experimental testing reveals that the proposed methodology is much more effective than the previously proposed methodology. This study focuses on comparison of unsupervised lexicon-based models (TextBlob, AFINN, Vader Sentiment) and supervised machine learning models (KNN, SVM, Random Forest and Naïve Bayes) for sentiment analysis. This is the first study with cyber public opinion over the abrogation of Article 370. Twitter data of more than 2 lakh tweets were collected by the authors. After cleaning, 29732 tweets were selected for analysis. As per the results among supervised learning, Random Forest performs the best, whereas among unsupervised learning TextBlob achieves the highest accuracy of 99 % and 88 %, respectively. Performance parameters of the proposed supervised machine learning models also surpass the result of the recent study performed in 2023 for sentiment analysis.
